Transforming events in flight

This guide covers how to reshape, filter, and enrich events as they pass through a pipeline — transforming raw data from your source into the exact shape your destination expects.

Reshaping event structure

A transform extracts fields from the incoming event and maps them to a new output structure. Use transforms to flatten nested data, rename fields, or select only the columns you need.

reshape-transform.json json 
{
  "transform": {
    "type": "jmespath",
    "expression": "{ id: user.id, email: user.contact.email, created: timestamp }"
  }
}

Filtering events

Filter out events that don't meet your criteria — for example, dropping test transactions or skipping events from staging environments. Filtered events are still recorded in the pipeline's audit log but do not reach your destination.

filter-transform.json json 
{
  "transform": {
    "type": "filter",
    "condition": "environment == 'production' && amount > 100"
  }
}
Filtered events are not lost

Filtered events skip the destination write but remain queryable in your pipeline's event history. Use the API to review what was filtered and when.

Enriching events

Add computed fields, lookups from external systems, or metadata to each event before it reaches your destination. Enrichments can call out to external APIs, query a database, or perform calculations on the event data.

enrich-transform.json json 
{
  "transform": {
    "type": "enrich",
    "lookup": {
      "service": "user-api",
      "key_field": "user_id",
      "output_fields": ["tier", "region", "last_login"]
    }
  }
}

Chaining multiple transforms

Transforms run in sequence — the output of one becomes the input to the next. This lets you filter first, reshape second, and enrich last, keeping your logic modular and testable.

Transform performance

Enrichments that call external services add latency. Consider caching results, using batch lookups, or pre-computing enrichments upstream of your pipeline if throughput is critical.

Testing transforms locally

Use the Pipelines endpoint to dry-run a transform against sample events before deploying it to production. This lets you validate your JMESPath expressions and filter conditions without risking live data.

Next steps

With your events shaped correctly, see Handling errors & retries to understand what happens when a transformed event fails to reach your destination.

Handling errors & retries

Every event that fails a transform or a destination write is retried automatically. This guide covers how that works and what to do when retries run out.

Automatic retries

Failed events retry with exponential backoff — 1s, 2s, 4s, up to a per-pipeline configurable ceiling. Most transient failures (a destination hiccup, a rate-limited third party) resolve within the first few attempts.

pipeline-retry-config.json json 
{
  "retry_policy": {
    "max_attempts": 5,
    "backoff": "exponential",
    "initial_delay_ms": 1000
  }
}

Dead-lettering

An event that exhausts its retries is moved to that pipeline's dead-letter queue rather than dropped silently.

Dead-lettered events don't retry themselves

Once in the dead-letter queue, an event stays there until you replay it or explicitly discard it — it will not retry again on its own.

Replaying events

Use the Events endpoint's replay action to re-run a specific dead-lettered event once the underlying issue is fixed.

replay.sh bash 
curl -X POST https://api.godzilladocs.dev/v2/events/evt_8f2c1a90/replay \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $GODZILLA_API_KEY"

Watching for failures

Subscribe to pipeline.failed via Webhooks so you find out about dead-lettered events before a customer does. See also Monitoring & alerts.

Scheduling & triggers

A pipeline runs either on a schedule or in response to incoming events. This guide covers both.

Scheduled pipelines

Set a schedule (a cron expression) when creating or updating a pipeline via the Pipelines endpoint. Godzilla runs the pipeline once per schedule tick, processing whatever new data is available from the source since the last run.

schedule.json json 
{
  "schedule": "0 */4 * * *"
}

Event-triggered pipelines

Omit schedule and the pipeline instead runs continuously, processing events as its source connector emits them — the right choice for sources like Kafka or a Webhook connector where near-real-time matters.

Choosing between them

Use a schedule for sources that batch naturally (a nightly file drop to S3). Use event-triggered for anything where minutes matter.

Pausing and resuming

A paused pipeline skips scheduled ticks entirely and buffers nothing for event-triggered sources — resuming picks up new events going forward, not a backlog. To reprocess a time range instead, see the replay flow in Handling errors & retries.

Monitoring & alerts

Keep an eye on a running pipeline without babysitting it manually.

Connector health

Poll a connector's health field via the Connectors endpoint, or better, subscribe to connector.error so you're notified the moment it degrades.

Subscribing to pipeline lifecycle events

The most reliable way to monitor a pipeline is a webhook subscription on pipeline.failed and connector.error.

subscribe.sh bash 
curl -X POST https://api.godzilladocs.dev/v2/webhooks \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $GODZILLA_API_KEY" \
  -d '{"url":"https://you.example.com/hooks/godzilla","events":["pipeline.failed","connector.error"]}'
Recommended baseline

At minimum, subscribe to pipeline.failed for every production pipeline. It's the single highest-signal event for catching problems before customers do.

Dead-letter queue depth

A growing dead-letter queue is an early warning sign, not just a symptom — see Handling errors & retries for how events end up there and how to drain them.
